title: Fashion yourself (137–145)
hookLine: irrigators lead water, fletchers bend arrows, carpenters bend wood; the good fashion themselves

lines: A POTTER, A GARDENER, A WOODWORKER.
cards: A potter centers clay on the wheel. A gardener trains a vine along a fence, a little each week. A woodworker steams a strip of oak until it will bend into the curve of a chair.
None of them fight the material. None of them finish in a day. They lead it, patiently, toward a shape.
The last verse of chapter ten gathers three craftsmen like that, and then adds a fourth, whose material is the self.

teach.b: First, chapter ten names what doesn't work.

Verse one forty-one lists the dramatic ascetic practices of the Buddha's day and says none of them purify anyone on their own: "Not nakedness, not platted hair, not dirt, not fasting, or lying on the earth, not rubbing with dust, not sitting motionless, can purify a mortal who has not overcome desires."
The traditional story of his life says the Buddha had tried severe austerities himself before his awakening, and set them aside. Show doesn't shape the mind.

teach.h: A HORSE THAT NEEDS ONLY A TOUCH.
teach.b: Then comes a well-trained horse that needs only a touch of the whip to get moving, and the text asks: is anyone that responsive to correction? Then the craftsmen.
Verse one forty-five: "Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; good people fashion themselves."

Müller says well-makers; the Pali word is often translated irrigators, the people who dig channels and lead water across fields. A fletcher is an arrow-maker, who heats and straightens a shaft until it flies true.
Almost the same verse appeared back in chapter six, verse eighty, about the wise. The Pali verb at the end means to tame or train, the way you'd train a young horse.
Together, the images make a quiet, practical picture of change.

teach.h: DIG A CHANNEL, NOT A WALL.
teach.b: Water isn't forced uphill; it's given a channel.
Wood isn't snapped; it's bent with heat and time. Habits aren't smashed either. You dig a small channel, and dig it again tomorrow.

how: Buddhist training is often described as gradual, like a craftsman's work: keeping precepts, sitting daily and guarding the senses, rather than dramatic acts of self-denial, which the Buddha is remembered as having tried and set aside.

o: force yourself into shape by sheer willpower
dress well so others see who you really are
train yourself patiently, like a craftsman

games.q: match each craftsman to the material.

s: verse 141 says fasting and sleeping on the ground purify the mind by themselves
it lists them and says none purify someone who hasn't overcome desires.
a near-twin of verse 145 appears in chapter six
verse 80, about the wise, uses the same three craftsmen.
the fletcher in the verse is an arrow-maker
he straightens and bends the shaft until it flies true.

games.q: you want to stop checking your phone first thing every morning. which approach fits verse 145?
o: throw the phone in a lake.
give the habit a new channel, like a book by the bed.
promise to never touch it again.
games.why: irrigators don't force water uphill; they lead it. the verse pictures change as patient shaping, not smashing.

practice: Choose one habit you'd like to shape, not overhaul: scrolling before bed, interrupting, skipping lunch.

Instead of fighting it, picture a small channel beside it, one easy thing that could carry the energy somewhere better, like a book by the pillow, one breath before speaking, or a piece of fruit in your bag.
Then let the picture go, and sit with the breath, bending gently toward stillness.

wordCard.voice: Fashion yourself. Verse one forty-five: irrigators lead water, fletchers bend arrows, carpenters bend wood, and good people shape themselves.

orig.note: Pali: taming, training, self-control — the root of the verb at the end of verse 145, where the good tame themselves.

carryVoice: Your line: water led in channels. Not forced, just led, patiently. Day one hundred eighty-six.
